tldr: The authors propose CrossSafe, a safety filter that reasons about risk prediction and safe avoidance using a shared model while accounting for differences in morphology and joint structure across robots, reducing collisions on unseen robots in a zero-shot manner without fine-tuning.
hero_caption: Overall architecture of CrossSafe. Safety features such as velocities are fused with tokens from the pretrained HoloBrain-0 model, and geometry-aware cross-attention incorporating 3D positions constructs a latent state. Based on this, a Hamilton-Jacobi (HJ) critic and safety actor operate across robots with varying degrees of freedom.
overview:
High-level safety reasoning, such as recognizing an obstacle and deciding to avoid it, should be largely shared across robots. However, when executing safe robot motions, differences in morphology—such as arm length, joint arrangement, and degrees of freedom (DoF)—present a major hurdle. Even with identical end-effector trajectories, an elbow might collide with an obstacle on one robot while staying completely clear on another.

To tackle this, the authors introduce a "cross-embodiment latent safety filter" learned as a single unified model that enforces safety across heterogeneous robots. CrossSafe builds a latent representation incorporating each link's 3D velocity, kinematics, and relative 3D distance and direction to the environment. It then learns a safety value function (critic) and an avoidance policy (actor) in this latent space based on Hamilton-Jacobi (HJ) reachability analysis.

The authors evaluate CrossSafe across five bimanual robot embodiments (Piper, Franka-Panda, ARX-X5, UR5-WSG, and Aloha-AgileX) and five manipulation tasks, measuring zero-shot generalization to embodiments held out during training. Crucially, they test whether a filter trained only on 6-DoF arms can transfer directly to an unseen 7-DoF Franka-Panda arm.

CrossSafe significantly reduces the nominal policy's collision rate on unseen robots and substantially lowers contact forces. Furthermore, training across more robot embodiments improves generalization to unseen robots, demonstrating that the scaling benefits of multi-embodiment learning apply to safety enforcement as well.
contributions: Proposed a Hamilton-Jacobi (HJ) reachability-based safety critic and actor that absorb morphological and kinematic differences and can be shared across robots with varying degrees of freedom.
Introduced a geometry-aware cross-attention mechanism that explicitly accounts for each link's 3D velocity and kinematics, as well as the 3D relative positions between links and scene patches.
Demonstrated zero-shot collision rate reduction on unseen robot embodiments across five bimanual robots and five manipulation tasks.
Showed that co-training across multiple embodiments improves generalization to unseen robots compared to training on a single embodiment alone.

sections.heading: Can robots with different bodies share a single safety filter?
sections.summary: Training separate models for every robot is costly, spurring cross-embodiment task learning. This paper extends that concept to safety filters, asking whether a filter trained on multiple robots can achieve zero-shot generalization on unseen embodiments.
sections.details:
Collecting platform-specific datasets to train individual models is prohibitively expensive as robot learning scales up. Recently, cross-embodiment learning frameworks like Open X-Embodiment and Octo have advanced rapidly, sharing task knowledge across heterogeneous robot morphologies.

However, most generalist manipulation policies operate in a shared end-effector action space (delta end-effector pose). Here lies the catch: even if two robots track identical end-effector paths, differences in link lengths and joint axes lead to completely different trajectories for their elbows and body links. An action that is safe for one robot can cause another to collide with obstacles.

Prior approaches like EmbodiSteer and Any-Body Guard recompute kinematics-based safety online for the target robot, but they do not learn a shared safety value function or avoidance policy across embodiments.

To address this, the authors propose CrossSafe, a framework that constructs a latent representation balancing shared safety reasoning with embodiment-specific morphology, learning a single HJ reachability-based safety critic and actor. Through leave-one-embodiment-out cross-validation across five bimanual robots and five manipulation tasks, they demonstrate for the first time that a shared filter can reduce collisions on unseen robots without fine-tuning.

sections.heading: At the intersection of multi-robot learning and control-theoretic safety
sections.summary: The paper surveys cross-embodiment policies and control-theoretic safety methods like control barrier functions and HJ reachability. It highlights the novelty of learning a shared safety value function explicitly conditioned on robot morphology.
sections.details:
This work bridges two primary research areas.

### II-A Cross-Embodiment Generalist Policies
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models such as OpenVLA, Octo, and HoloBrain-0 train across multi-robot datasets, accommodating hardware differences via prompting, URDF files, or kinematic graphs. Many works targeting zero-shot transfer (like LAP or Cloak) emphasize embodiment-invariant representations. For safety control, however, the robot's physical structure directly dictates which actions are safe; making representations strictly embodiment-invariant strips away the morphology needed to avoid collisions. A representation must generalize while preserving morphology.

### II-B Latent Safety Filters and Safe Control
Control Barrier Functions (CBFs) and Hamilton-Jacobi (HJ) reachability analysis provide formal frameworks for safety. Combining these with reinforcement learning allows safety value functions to be learned over high-dimensional observations or latent spaces (latent safety filters). However, existing works focus on generalizing across language instructions or environment variations, not across heterogeneous robot embodiments. Unlike methods that compute full geometric collision checks online at runtime, this approach amortizes safety reasoning via offline learning inside the model.

sections.heading: HJ reachability basics and scaling with reinforcement learning
sections.summary: This section reviews the mathematics of Hamilton-Jacobi (HJ) reachability analysis for identifying safe sets. It explains how reinforcement learning (SAC) solves the HJ Bellman equation in continuous action spaces to overcome the curse of dimensionality.
sections.details:
Let the system state be $s_t$, the action be $a_t$, and the transition dynamics be $s_{t+1}=f(s_t,a_t)$. The failure set to avoid is defined as $\mathcal{F}:=\{s\mid h(s)<0\}$, where $h(s)$ is a margin function representing quantities like distance to obstacles.

The goal of HJ reachability analysis is to compute the optimal value function that guarantees remaining outside $\mathcal{F}$ over an infinite horizon: $V(s):=\sup_{\pi}\inf_{t\geq 0}h(\xi_s^\pi(t))$. This satisfies the dynamic programming fixed-point condition:
$$V(s)=\min\left\{h(s),\max_{a\in A}V(f(s,a))\right\}$$
The set where $V(s)<0$ is the Backward Reachable Set (BRS); once inside it, entering a failure state is inevitable under any policy.

Because analytical solutions are intractable for high-dimensional manipulators, the authors approximate the HJ safety critic $Q_\theta(s,a)$ using reinforcement learning (Soft Actor-Critic). Specifically, the network is optimized on transition data by minimizing the mean squared error against the target $y_t$:
$$y_t := (1-\gamma)h(s_t) + \gamma\min\left\{h(s_t),\max_{a\in A}Q_\theta(s_{t+1},a)\right\}$$
where $\gamma\in(0,1)$ is a discount factor. This allows data-driven optimization of the safety value function in continuous action spaces.

sections.heading: Inside CrossSafe: Embedding geometry and kinematics into a safe latent space
sections.summary: This section covers the core components of CrossSafe: augmenting HoloBrain-0 representations with safety features like 3D velocities and depths, and introducing geometry-aware cross-attention to handle robots with varying degrees of freedom.
sections.details:
CrossSafe relies on four key architectural designs:

### IV-A Leveraging Frozen HoloBrain-0
For visual and robot state encoding, a pretrained and frozen HoloBrain-0 (GroundingDINO variant) is used. It extracts 3D scene patch tokens $\mathbf{c}$ and their 3D coordinates $\mathbf{p}^{\textit{scene}}$ from camera inputs, alongside initial link tokens $\hat{\mathbf{z}}$ computed via forward kinematics from joint angles. Using 3D link poses rather than raw joint angles avoids sensitivity to differing joint origin definitions across robots.

### IV-B Augmenting with Safety Features
Because HoloBrain-0 processes single static frames, it lacks velocity information critical for collision avoidance. For each link $i$, the authors build a safety feature vector $b_i$ containing 3D linear and angular velocities (derived via the Jacobian), arm-length-normalized positions and orientations, depth $\delta_i$ in the kinematic tree, and a left/right arm indicator $\chi_i$. This vector is concatenated and projected via an MLP with the HoloBrain-0 token to form the initial link token $z_i^{(0)}$.

### IV-C Geometry-Aware Manipulator-Scene Attention
Standard cross-attention relies solely on feature similarity. In collision avoidance, however, knowing the relative 3D distance and direction to obstacles from each link is crucial. CrossSafe injects the Euclidean distance $d_{ij}$ and unit direction vector $\hat{r}_{ij}$ between links and scene patches in world coordinates as attention score biases, explicitly concatenating directional information to the output tokens.

### IV-D Critic and Safety Policy Architecture
The safety actor directly predicts per-joint displacements from the link tokens. Predicting joint-level actions rather than end-effector deltas enables fine-grained whole-body collision avoidance. The safety critic predicts the perturbed link positions $dp_i, dw_i$ under a candidate action, processes them through an action-conditioned geometry-aware layer, and computes per-link safety scores. These link scores are aggregated via a smooth minimum to yield the robot's overall safety value.

sections.heading: Experimental setup: 5 bimanual robots and leave-one-out validation
sections.summary: Details the experimental protocol using five bimanual robots (e.g., Piper, Franka-Panda) and five tasks in RoboTwin 2.0. The setup rigorously compares performance on trained robots (InD) and zero-shot held-out robots (OOD).
sections.details:
### V-A Experimental Setup
Evaluations use RoboTwin 2.0 across five bimanual robots: Piper, ARX-X5, UR5-WSG, Aloha-AgileX, and Franka-Panda. Franka-Panda has 7 DoF per arm, whereas the other four have 6 DoF per arm. Tasks include five bimanual manipulation challenges (e.g., "put bread into basket", "stack blocks"). A static obstacle (a drink carton) is placed along the nominal trajectory. Because the nominal planner (cuRobo) ignores the obstacle, it collides with high probability without intervention. The safety margin $h(s)$ is the minimum signed distance between the obstacle and all robot collision spheres and gripped objects.

### V-B Training and Online Intervention
The model is trained via SAC using an offline buffer collected across tasks and robots. At runtime (25 Hz), the critic evaluates nominal action $a_{\text{nom}}$. If $Q_\theta(\mathbf{z},a_{\text{nom}})\geq 0$, the nominal action executes; if negative (unsafe), the safety actor intervenes with $a_{\text{safe}}$. Total inference time is around 73 ms.

### V-C Baselines and Metrics
Baselines include ablations without safety features (w/o Aug), without geometric attention bias (w/o Geo), without both, and X-VLA-Safe (built on the X-VLA backbone). Metrics include Collision Rate (CR), Success Rate (SR), Intervention Rate (IR), and Contact Force. A 5-fold Leave-One-Embodiment-Out cross-validation scheme evaluates generalization, training on four robots and testing zero-shot on the held-out (OOD) robot.

sections.heading: Zero-shot transfer reduces collisions on an unseen 7-DoF robot
sections.summary: CrossSafe lowers the collision rate by roughly 14 percentage points on unseen robots and significantly reduces contact force. Key findings include successful transfer from 6-DoF models to a 7-DoF robot and clear advantages over single-embodiment specialist models.
sections.details:
### Improved Safety Across Robots and Tasks with a Single Filter
While the unconstrained nominal controller suffered a 64.1% collision rate (CR), CrossSafe reduced it to 39.8% on in-distribution (InD) robots and 49.8% on out-of-distribution (OOD) robots. Peak contact force dropped from 179.6 N (nominal) to 113.6 N (InD) and 102.9 N (OOD).

### Generalization to an Unseen 7-DoF Arm (Franka-Panda)
The most notable test was zero-shot transfer of a model trained exclusively on four 6-DoF arms to the 7-DoF Franka-Panda. Despite the shift in kinematics and action dimensions, CrossSafe lowered Franka-Panda's CR from 66.0% to 60.4% (reducing collisions in 4 out of 5 tasks) while raising success rate (SR) from 40.4% to 45.2%. In contrast, ablations lacking geometric biases or velocity features saw collision rates surge to 76%–79%, showing these components are essential for cross-DoF generalization.

### Comparison with X-VLA-Safe and Specialist Models
X-VLA-Safe, which operates in end-effector space, achieved minimal collision reductions and cut task success rates roughly in half (~48% drop) because end-effector control cannot effectively prevent whole-body link collisions.
Moreover, comparing generalist filters trained on four embodiments against specialist filters trained on a single embodiment revealed that generalists outperformed specialists across all OOD metrics: lower CR (49.8% vs. 54.4%), higher SR (29.4% vs. 27.0%), and lower contact force (102.9 N vs. 144.8 N). Exposure to diverse morphologies builds more robust safety reasoning for unseen robots.

sections.heading: Conclusion and future directions: Toward physical hardware and guarantees
sections.summary: CrossSafe proves that a single safety filter can transfer across robots with different DoFs via morphology-aware tokenization. While learning-based methods lack absolute guarantees, future work looks toward conformal prediction and physical deployment.
sections.details:
Based on the hypothesis that high-level safety reasoning is shared while realization depends on morphology, this work introduced CrossSafe with morphology-aware tokens and geometry-aware attention. Simulated evaluations confirmed improved safety on unseen bimanual robots—even across differing DoFs—without fine-tuning.

However, clear limitations remain:
First, being a learning-based filter, it cannot provide strict mathematical zero-collision guarantees like traditional analytical HJ reachability, leaving residual collisions.
Second, experiments were conducted entirely in simulation (RoboTwin 2.0) without physical hardware validation.

Future directions include integrating conformal prediction or scenario optimization for probabilistic safety guarantees, handling dynamic obstacles and broader robot morphologies, and validating the approach on real-world hardware platforms.

sections.heading: Appendix: Implementation details and hyperparameters
sections.summary: Covers simulation setup details, obstacle generation logic, training hyperparameters for SAC with Twin Critics, and the inference latency breakdown across model components.
sections.details:
### Simulation Setup and Tasks
Simulations run in RoboTwin 2.0 (based on SAPIEN) at 250 Hz physics and a 25 Hz control loop ($\Delta t=0.04$ s). Episodes last up to 450 control steps (18 seconds). The obstacle is a box model sized approximately $11.0\times 15.4\times 11.6$ cm placed randomly along the straight line connecting the pick and place locations. It appears on the path with probability 0.7 during training and 1.0 during evaluation.

### Training and Inference Specifics
The critic uses a Twin Critic architecture to prevent value overestimation. Training employs SAC with temperature $T=0.4$, batch size 64, learning rate $3\times 10^{-4}$, and discount factor $\gamma=0.9$. The safety actor outputs Gaussian parameters via linear layers over joint tokens, mapped through $\tanh$ to $[-1, 1]$ and scaled by per-joint velocity limits.

On an NVIDIA A40 GPU, HoloBrain-0 feature extraction takes ~59.8 ms, and CrossSafe modules take ~13.1 ms, yielding an overall inference time of ~73.0 ms (~13.7 Hz).

takeaways: Directly predicting joint-level link displacements rather than end-effector deltas is critical for whole-body collision avoidance during cross-embodiment transfer.
Injecting relative 3D distances and direction vectors between robot links and scene patches directly as attention biases drives effective geometric generalization to unseen embodiments.
Just like generalist task policies, safety filters gain stronger generalization to unseen robots when co-trained across multiple embodiments rather than trained as single-robot specialists.
limitations: As a learning-based filter, it lacks deterministic safety guarantees (zero collisions), leaving a residual rate of collisions.
Evaluations are restricted to the RoboTwin 2.0 simulator; real-world testing subject to camera calibration error and sensor noise has not yet been conducted.
Obstacles are limited to single static objects; extending the framework to dynamic obstacles and complex open-world environments remains future work.
